subject: Jacobians, CDFs, inverse CDFs, and PDFs

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Jacobians, CDFs, inverse CDFs, and PDFs
parts:
Everyone's always saying they find Jacobians hard. It really really
helped me to work through a few examples. This one's very generic
and has the side effect of reinforcing the definition of a density
as the derivative of the cdf.

Suppose

Y ~ uniform(0, 1)

and you map that to

Z = normal_inverse_cdf(Y)

assuming that's the inverse of a standard normal (i.e., normal(0, 1))
cumulative density function. Now you can do that in R: draw a bunch of Y,
apply the normal inverse CDF, plot the result as a histogram. It
should look like a standard normal, not like a uniform. The Jacobian
is what lets us calculate that density.

How do we calculate the density of Z? We apply the inverse
map back to Y, then multiply by the absolute Jacobian of that
inverse map, which is just the absolute derivative in one dimension.

The inverse of normal_inverse_cdf is just normal_cdf, so everything
cancels neatly:

p_Z(z) = p_Y(std_normal_cdf(z)) * d/dz | std_normal_cdf(z) |

= 1 * normal(z)

which is just what you want.

It works in general for any continuous CDF because the derivative
of a CDF is just the PDF. Really the CDFs are much more primitive---they're
what relate to probabilities. Densities just give you something
convenient to integrate to get back to probaiblities.

Too bad we don't have the inverse CDFs in Stan. Maybe after
we add a root finder ...

- Bob

P.S. It's even easier with the standard logistic, because the inverse
cdf is just inverse logit, or 1 / (1 + exp(-u)). Differentiating
that is where the logistic pdf comes from.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobians, CDFs, inverse CDFs, and PDFs
parts:
That's fun---I love math at the chalkboard in theorem-example
style. It's just so much easier to make out when it's presented
a symbol at a time.

I thought his use of dx/dy was clean but potentially confusing. I
wrestled with that issue writing the manual. I was like a kid
at the movies, hoping our hero would write out the second line of

P_Y(y) = P_X(x) d.x / d.y

= P_X(g^{-1}(y)) d.g^{-1}(y) / d.y

here, Y = g(X) is the transform, where g is monotonically increasingy
and continuously differentiable.

- Bob
